scimon.text: Consider the following context: High-temperature self-lubricating materials with stable tribological performance across a wide temperature range are essential for advanced mechanical systems under extreme conditions. However, balancing mechanical strength and lubrication efficiency remains a key challenge. In that context, which material can be used for high-performance wide-temperature self-lubricating materials, and why?

hidden_target.material_initial_state: Uniformly ball-milled powder mixtures containing 67.5 wt.% CoCrFeNiMox high-entropy-alloy matrix powder (x = 0.2, 0.5, or 1), 12.5 wt.% Ni-coated MoS2 composite powder, 15 wt.% Ag, and 5 wt.% Cr2O3; the powders were mixed at 150 r/min for 8 h before sintering.
hidden_target.intervention: Mo content in CoCrFeNiMox-Ni/MoS2-Ag-Cr2O3 composites was varied from x = 0.2 to 0.5 and 1, and the resulting SPS-fabricated composites were compared in phase constitution, microstructure, compression properties, hardness, and wide-temperature tribological behavior.
hidden_target.conditions: Spark plasma sintering was performed under vacuum and 40 MPa by heating to 1250 °C at 150 °C/min, holding for 3 min, and furnace cooling. Ball-on-disk tests were conducted in air at room temperature, 200, 400, 600, and 800 °C against a 6 mm Si3N4 ball, using an 8 N load, 4 mm rotation radius, 0.15 m/s sliding speed, and 270 m sliding distance. Vickers hardness used a 300 g load for 10 s; compression tests used 4 mm × 8 mm specimens at 1 mm/min.
hidden_target.structural_mediator: Increasing Mo produced Mo-induced FCC lattice distortion and increasing amounts of a hard, Mo-rich tetragonal σ phase, while Ag, Ni/MoS2, and Cr2O3 remained distributed mainly along matrix-powder boundaries. During sliding, Ni/MoS2-Ag-rich lubricating films operated at low-to-medium temperature, whereas oxide/molybdate tribofilms formed at high temperature; Mo1 developed a particularly continuous, dense glaze at 800 °C containing NiO and Ag2MoO4, Ag2Mo4O13, and Ag2Mo2O7.
hidden_target.mechanism: Dissolved Mo impedes dislocation motion through solid-solution strengthening, and the hard σ phase suppresses plastic deformation and scratching through second-phase strengthening. At lower temperatures, layered MoS2 supplies a low-shear film and soft Ag reduces adhesion, although thermal softening and rough wear tracks at 200–400 °C hinder formation of a continuous lubricant layer. At 600–800 °C, oxidation and tribochemical reactions generate layered silver molybdates and other oxides; compaction of these products into a glaze separates the matrix from the counterface and reduces interfacial shear and material removal.
hidden_target.predicted_outcome: Relative to the Mo0.2 composite, increasing Mo was predicted to increase hardness and generally improve wear resistance through lattice distortion and σ-phase formation, while high-temperature oxide/molybdate glaze formation was predicted to lower friction and wear relative to the intermediate-temperature condition. The highest-Mo Mo1 composition was expected to provide the best strength/wear balance, although not necessarily the lowest coefficient of friction at every temperature.
hidden_target.baseline: The principal compositional baseline was Mo0.2, which was predominantly an FCC solid solution with Ag, Ni/MoS2, and Cr2O3 and little detectable σ phase. Its hardness, yield strength, and plastic strain were 432 HV, 445 MPa, and 15%, respectively; its friction coefficient was 0.66 at room temperature, peaked at 0.75 at 200 °C, and fell to about 0.21 at 800 °C. Its wear rate was 13.1 × 10^-6 mm3/N·m at room temperature, 98.1 × 10^-6 mm3/N·m at 400 °C, and 6.6 × 10^-6 mm3/N·m at 800 °C.
hidden_target.boundary: The tribological conclusions apply to dry sliding in air against Si3N4 from room temperature to 800 °C under the specified 8 N, 0.15 m/s, 270 m test. Abrasive wear dominated near room temperature; abrasive/adhesive or abrasive/oxidative wear and thermal softening governed 200–400 °C; oxidative wear and molybdate-film formation governed 600–800 °C. Mo0.5 generally had the lowest friction except at 600 °C, whereas Mo1 gave the lowest wear and most coherent glaze at 800 °C.
hidden_target.discriminating_measurement: XRD peak shifts and σ-phase peaks, SEM/EDS phase and wear-track mapping, Vickers hardness and compression stress–strain measurements, temperature-dependent coefficient of friction, profilometry-derived wear-scar dimensions and wear rate, and Raman identification of the Mo1 wear-surface glaze after testing at 800 °C.
hidden_target.actual_result: Mo0.5 and Mo1 showed detectable σ phase and greater lattice distortion than Mo0.2. Hardness increased from 432 HV for Mo0.2 to 488 HV for Mo0.5 and 546 HV for Mo1; yield strength peaked at 502 MPa for Mo0.5 versus 445 MPa for Mo0.2 and 443 MPa for Mo1, while plastic strains were 15%, 10%, and 17%, respectively. Friction peaked at 200 °C and decreased toward 800 °C for all compositions; the minimum reported coefficient was 0.23 for Mo0.5 at 800 °C, while Mo1 reached 0.26. Wear peaked at 400 °C and then declined: Mo1 decreased from 73.5 × 10^-6 mm3/N·m at 400 °C to 3.15 × 10^-6 mm3/N·m at 800 °C, where its continuous NiO/silver-molybdate glaze yielded the best combined wear resistance and low friction. The paper's blanket statements that all wear rates were below 10^-5 mm3/N·m, and the abstract's claim of below 10^-6 mm3/N·m, conflict with its tabulated/graph-reported 400 °C values of 73.5–98.1 × 10^-6 mm3/N·m.
